interactive.title: The arrow and its shadows
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Twelve small screens share one grid and one solid arrow, from its tail at the origin to its tip. Its two parts are drawn dashed, nose to tail. The across part runs along the x-axis. The up part climbs from there to the tip. They meet at a right angle, so they close a right-angled triangle with the arrow as its long side. A readout shows the parts as a column and as i and j. Here i is the unit vector along the x-axis, and j the unit vector up the y-axis. Dragging the tip changes the arrow, and the dashed parts follow it. With a size and an angle, the triangle gives the parts. The side next to the angle is the size times the angle's cosine. The side opposite is the size times its sine. A label on each dashed side says which. North is up the page and east along the x-axis. A switch moves the angle marker from off the x-axis to a bearing, measured clockwise from north. The arrow and its parts stay put. The angle now sits next to the north side, so the cos label jumps to that side. Going back, the size is Pythagoras on the parts. A 3-D switch tips the grid back into a floor. A third axis, z, stands up at right angles to it, with k the unit vector along it. The arrow stands in a box whose edges are its i, j and k parts, and dragging turns the box. Its size is Pythagoras twice: across the floor, then up. The screens: arrow a, 3 across and 4 up. A puzzle on an arrow 4 across and 2 down. A 10 N pull at 30° off the x-axis, with an angle slider from 0° to 90°. A puzzle on a 20 N pull at 60°. The bearing switch on the 10 N pull. A puzzle on 12 knots on a bearing of 030. The arrow −3i + 4j and its angle. A puzzle on the size of 5i − 12j. The box for 2i + 3j + 6k. A puzzle on the size of 4i + 4j + 7k. Two mixed puzzles: a ring on one rope with its parts drawn, and a 50 N winch rope on a bearing of 120. Some screens show an idea, and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is drawn so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The grid's squares have no unit, so one arrow can stand for newtons, knots or metres. The parts here always lie along the x and y axes. A vector can be split along any two lines at right angles, such as along and across a slope. Turning the 3-D box changes only your view. The arrow and its parts stay the same. The puzzles use example values, and parts are rounded to two decimal places.

explain.text:
Any vector can be split into two parts at right angles, one along each axis. Those parts are its [[component]]s, the separate x, y and z values of the vector.[^1] Take the arrow a again, 3 across and 4 up. Its across part runs along the x-axis. Its up part climbs from there to the tip. Drawn nose to tail, the two parts end exactly at the arrow's tip. So together they are the arrow, described along the axes, not extra pulls. The parts and the arrow close a right-angled triangle, with the arrow as the long side. You write the parts as a column, 3 above 4, or as 3i + 4j. Here i is the unit vector along the x-axis and j is the unit vector up the y-axis. So 3i + 4j means 3 lots of i, then 4 lots of j.

Often you know the size and an angle instead. Then the triangle gives the parts. Take a 10 N pull at 30° above the x-axis. The angle sits between the arrow and the across side. In a right-angled triangle, the side next to an angle is the long side times the angle's cosine. So the across part is 10 cos 30° = 8.66 N. The side opposite the angle is the long side times its sine, so the up part is 10 sin 30° = 5 N. Finding the parts this way is called [[resolving]] the pull. Each part is shorter than the arrow, unless the arrow lies along an axis. Then one part is the whole arrow and the other is zero. A bearing shows why it matters which side is next to the angle. Put north up the page and east along the x-axis. A bearing is measured clockwise from north. The pull sits 30° above east, so it is 60° round from north, a bearing of 060. Now the angle sits next to the north side, so north takes the cosine: 10 cos 60° = 5 N. East takes the sine: 10 sin 60° = 8.66 N. The parts have not changed. Only the angle moved, and the cos went with it.

Going back, the size is Pythagoras on the parts, not the parts added. The pull's parts give √(8.66² + 5²) = 10 N, not 13.66 N. The angle comes from the tangent, but check the signs. For −3i + 4j a calculator's tan⁻¹(4 ÷ −3) gives −53.13°, which points right and down. The signs say left and up, so add 180° to get 126.87°. A third axis, z, stands at right angles to both, and k is the unit vector along it. 2i + 3j + 6k runs 2 across, 3 along and 6 up. Across the floor, Pythagoras gives √(2² + 3²) = √13. The 6 up stands at right angles to that floor line, so Pythagoras again gives √(13 + 6²) = √49 = 7. Parts along one axis add and take away as plain numbers.[^1] That is what makes adding vectors easy.

**A vector's components are its parts along the axes, written ai + bj + ck. The part next to the given angle is the size times its cosine, the other is the size times its sine, and the size comes back by Pythagoras.**

analogy.text: Your power triangle is the same split. Say a load draws 10 kVA at a power factor of 0.8. The active power is the side next to the angle φ: 10 × 0.8 = 8 kW. The reactive power is the side opposite: 10 × 0.6 = 6 kvar, since sin φ is 0.6 when cos φ is 0.8. Pythagoras takes you back to 10 kVA, and 8 + 6 = 14 means nothing.
analogy.breaks: The angle φ is a shift in time between current and voltage, not a direction in space. So the power triangle has no third axis and nothing like k.

practice.text:
- Draw the arrow and its two parts nose to tail, so they close a right-angled triangle.
- Mark the given angle. The side next to it is the size times cos. The other side is the size times sin.
- With an angle off the x-axis, across is size × cos θ and up is size × sin θ. With a bearing, east is size × sin θ and north is size × cos θ.
- Give each part its sign. Left and down are minus, and so are west and south.
- Check that Pythagoras on the parts gives back the size.
- Going back to an angle, use the tangent, then check the quarter from the signs.

**Rule of thumb:** Cos goes on the side next to the angle.

**Worked example:** A submarine makes 8 knots on a bearing of 210. East is 8 sin 210° = −4 knots. North is 8 cos 210° = −6.93 knots. So its velocity is −4i − 6.93j. Both parts are minus, so it heads south and west, as 210 should. Check: √(4² + 6.93²) = √64 = 8 knots.

**Common mistakes**
- Putting sin next to the angle. With a bearing, the angle sits next to north, so north takes cos.
- Giving a part the arrow's whole size. That only happens when the arrow lies along that axis.
- Adding the parts for the size. 5i − 12j has size 13, not 17.
- Writing the parts the wrong way round. 4i − 2j is 4 across and 2 down, not −2i + 4j.
- Trusting tan⁻¹ without the signs. −3i + 4j points at 126.87°, not −53.13°.
- Leaving k out of the size. 4i + 4j + 7k has size 9.
- Counting the parts as extra pulls. A ring on one rope feels one pull.

sources.quote: Vector components describe the separate x, y and z values of a vector. When working with vectors, components can be added or subtracted separately.
